Gertrude is the Queen of Denmark in William Shakespeare's Hamlet, whose hasty marriage to her murdered husband's brother Claudius sets the tragedy in motion. Her ambiguous moral status—whether complicit, knowing, or tragically blind—has made her one of literature's most debated figures. She represents the corruption of the royal court and the collision between maternal bond and feminine agency.

A widow who marries her brother-in-law Claudius within weeks of her first husband's death, she scandalizes the court and offends Hamlet. Her marriage suggests either her knowledge of the murder, her innocence and manipulation, or her inability to resist political pressure. Shakespeare leaves this deliberately ambiguous. She represents the feminine figure trapped between male authority: she obeys her father, then her husband, then her son, never controlling her own agency.

In the final duel scene, she drinks poison meant for Hamlet and dies with her son. This accidental death underscores her tragic entrapment. Hamlet conflates his disgust at his mother's sexuality with his rage at her betrayal, complicating the play's gender politics. Her role as the bridge between Hamlet and Claudius makes her central to the play's action despite relatively few lines. Much of her character is created through what others say about her. She embodies the powerlessness of women navigating courts where their bodies and choices are contested ground, where every decision—to remarry, to love, to speak—carries the weight of a kingdom's judgment.
